lesson.title: The Truth You're Trying to Estimate: Population Parameters
lesson.summary: This section defines a parameter as a fixed numeric characteristic of an entire population, contrasts it with a sample based statistic, and revisits the Lincoln High sleep example to show how a sample statistic estimates an unknown parameter.
lesson.body:
A parameter is a numeric characteristic that describes an entire population: a fixed, specific number, even if nobody actually knows its exact value. The population proportion of Lincoln High students who are female, calculated in an earlier section as 625 divided by 1,200, or approximately 52.1 percent, is a parameter, because it was computed using every single member of the population. Other common parameters include the population mean, usually written using the Greek letter mu, and the population proportion, usually written using the letter p. Statisticians favor Greek letters and specific symbols for parameters precisely to keep them visually distinct from the sample based numbers introduced in the previous section.

Here is the essential contrast to hold onto. A parameter describes the population and is a single fixed number, even when that number is unknown. A statistic, by comparison, describes a sample and is calculated directly from whatever data was actually collected. Because a sample changes depending on which individuals happen to be selected, a statistic can change from one sample to the next, while the underlying parameter it is trying to estimate never changes at all. The population's true mean height does not shift depending on which 10 students a researcher happens to survey, even though the sample mean calculated from those 10 students absolutely does shift depending on the selection.

Return to the Lincoln High sleep example from the previous section. The true average number of hours slept per night, across all 1,200 currently enrolled students, is a parameter. Statisticians commonly write this unknown population mean as mu. Nobody in that example ever measured all 1,200 students, so the exact value of mu remains unknown. What the researcher actually calculated was the sample mean, written as x bar, based on the random sample of 10 students who reported 7, 6, 8, 7, 5, 9, 6, 7, 8, and 7 hours of sleep. As calculated previously, that sample mean equals 70 divided by 10, or exactly 7.0 hours. The number 7.0 is a statistic, not a parameter, and it serves as an estimate of the unknown parameter mu, the true population mean, rather than being that parameter itself.

This distinction, between a fixed but often unknown parameter and a variable, calculable statistic, is one of the most important ideas in all of statistics, because so much of the field is really about answering one question: how good of an estimate does a sample statistic give of its corresponding population parameter, and how confident can we be in that estimate. Every earlier idea in this course, data, variables, observations, datasets, categorical and quantitative variables, populations, and samples, exists to support exactly this kind of question. Understanding what a parameter is, and recognizing that it is almost always the real, hidden target behind a statistical study, completes the foundational vocabulary this course set out to build.
